name: Functional Groups: Haloalkanes, Amines and Alcohols
what: This subtopic covers the structural features, IUPAC naming and classification of haloalkanes (fluoro-, chloro-, bromo-, iodo-), primary amines and alcohols (primary, secondary and tertiary), including drawing all three types of formula representations.
why: These three functional group families appear widely in pharmaceuticals, industrial solvents and biological molecules. Knowing how to identify, name and classify them is essential for the organic reactions topics that follow.

items.title: I can name haloalkanes using IUPAC rules, specifying the halogen type and its position on the chain
items.what: Haloalkane names use the prefixes fluoro-, chloro-, bromo- or iodo- before the parent alkane name. The chain is numbered from the end closest to the halogen to give it the lowest locant, and di-, tri-, tetra- prefixes are used for multiple identical halogens.
items.why: Haloalkanes are used as refrigerants, solvents and in pharmaceutical synthesis. Correct naming is needed to communicate precise structural information about which carbon bears the halogen.
items.example: CH3CHClCH2CH3 is named 2-chlorobutane because the chlorine is on the second carbon of a 4-carbon chain, and the chain is numbered from the end closest to the chlorine.

items.title: I can draw the structural, semi-structural and skeletal formulas of haloalkanes from their IUPAC names
items.what: Working from a haloalkane name, draw the parent carbon chain, attach the halogen symbol at the stated carbon position and complete the hydrogen count so each carbon has four bonds.
items.why: Drawing haloalkanes accurately from names is tested directly in exams and is needed before studying nucleophilic substitution reactions in later units.
items.example: 2-fluoro-3-methylpentane has a 5-carbon parent chain with F on carbon 2 and a methyl branch on carbon 3. In the skeletal formula, F is drawn at the second vertex and a one-carbon branch at the third.

items.title: I can distinguish between primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols based on their carbon structure
items.what: The classification depends on how many alkyl groups (R groups) are bonded to the carbon bearing the –OH group. One alkyl group (or none) gives a primary alcohol, two gives secondary and three gives tertiary.
items.why: The type of alcohol affects how it reacts in oxidation reactions, which is a major topic in Unit 4. Correctly classifying an alcohol is therefore needed for predicting its reaction products.
items.example: Propan-2-ol is a secondary alcohol because its central carbon carries the –OH group and is bonded to two other carbon-containing groups (two CH3 groups).

items.title: I can name primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols using IUPAC rules up to C8
items.what: Alcohol names are formed by replacing the terminal '-e' of the parent alkane name with '-ol'. The position of the –OH group is stated as a number before '-ol', and the chain is numbered from the end closest to the –OH group.
items.why: Precise naming of alcohols is required to distinguish between isomers with different properties and reactivities, and forms the basis for naming esters and other derivatives.
items.example: An alcohol with a 7-carbon chain, a methyl group on carbon 6 and the –OH on carbon 3 (numbered from the –OH end) is named 6-methylheptan-3-ol.

items.title: I can draw the structural, semi-structural and skeletal formulas of alcohols from their IUPAC names
items.what: Working from an alcohol name, draw the parent chain, place the –OH at the stated position and add any alkyl branches, remembering to show the O–H hydrogen in skeletal formulas since it is bonded to a non-carbon atom.
items.why: Drawing correct alcohol structures is an assessed skill and is needed for understanding intermolecular forces and boiling point trends discussed in the physical properties section.
items.example: 2,5-dimethylhexan-1-ol has a 6-carbon parent chain with –OH at carbon 1 and methyl branches at carbons 2 and 5. The skeletal formula shows –OH at the end vertex with branches at the second and fifth vertices.

items.title: I can name primary amines using IUPAC rules and draw their structural, semi-structural and skeletal formulas
items.what: Primary amine names replace the terminal '-e' of the parent alkane name with '-amine'. The position of the –NH2 group is stated before '-amine', and the chain is numbered from the end closest to the amino group.
items.why: Amines are the basis of amino acids and many pharmaceuticals, and their naming follows the same logic as alcohols, reinforcing the systematic approach to IUPAC nomenclature.
items.example: 4,4-dimethylpentan-2-amine has a 5-carbon parent chain with –NH2 on carbon 2 and two methyl groups on carbon 4. The skeletal formula shows NH2 at the second vertex and two branches at the fourth.
